system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 30 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Mission: Search for actionable dependencies created by loss of tumor suppressors or other loss-of-function alterations, beyond the paralog pairs.

Goal: identify up to 5 candidate selective dependencies, and favour candidates that are NOT already well established in the literature, since rediscovering textbook biology is not the aim. Pre-register, replicate, and submit honest findings, including failures.

input.mechanism: RB1-deficient cells lose the pRB-E2F checkpoint and rely on remaining cell-cycle control nodes; DYRK1A regulates DREAM complex assembly (LIN52 phosphorylation), cyclin D turnover and p27 stability. Without pRB, DREAM/p130-mediated repression and DYRK1A-controlled cell-cycle/transcriptional balance may become essential to avoid replication stress or to sustain proliferation. Signal is consistent across lung, bladder, uterus, CNS, bone (not lineage-driven).

KEAP1 loss constitutively activates NRF2, which rewires NADPH production and lipid metabolism; NRF2-high cells consume NADPH/glutathione for redox defense and may depend on de novo fatty-acid synthesis (FASN) for membrane lipids/lipid saturation to resist peroxidation. Signal holds within lung (NSCLC) and when leaving out lung.

BAP1 loss (mesothelioma, RCC) derepresses PRC1/H2AK119ub targets and alters polarity/epithelial programs; atypical PKC iota (PRKCI) drives polarity and oncogenic signaling (e.g., YAP, SOX2, ECT2/RAC1). BAP1-deficient cells may rely on PKCiota-driven signaling. Effect persists leaving out pleura. Small n (9).

In RB1-null cells, deregulated activator E2Fs drive proliferation; E2F3 is the key activator whose loss suppresses Rb-null phenotypes in mouse genetics, so RB1-mutant cancer cells become addicted to E2F3. Consistent across 5 lineages.

NF2/Merlin loss causes mitotic/ploidy defects and chromosomal instability; such cells may depend on p31comet (MAD2L1BP) together with TRIP13 (2nd-ranked hit) to silence the spindle assembly checkpoint and exit mitosis, avoiding prolonged arrest. Small n (13), partly cervical-driven; exploratory.

input.summary:
I searched for dependencies created by tumor-suppressor loss, skipping the known paralog pairs (SMARCA4→SMARCA2, ARID1A→ARID1B, STAG2→STAG1, CREBBP→EP300, and the paralog pairs that dominate the LOSS list). I also skipped other textbook or confounded signals: the TP53→p53-pathway hits, MTAP→PRMT5/MAT2A, KEAP1→NFE2L2, MSI-type mutations→WRN, and ATM→HCFC1R1, which tracks hypermutated melanoma and endometrial lines. MTAP loss→PELO was also skipped because PELO is broadly essential. I registered five hypotheses and two replicated.
(1) RB1 mutation→DYRK1A replicated, but only modestly in Sanger. Held-out Broad lines gave t=-4.9 (p=6e-7). Sanger gave t=-2.5 (p=0.007), and there the gene's effect is small: -0.10 vs +0.04 in other lines. A small PubMed search found no direct prior report of this pairing, so I'm treating it as possibly new, not established.
(2) RB1 mutation→E2F3 replicated strongly: held-out t=-10.3, Sanger t=-6.9. This is partially known from mouse genetics.
Three exploratory candidates failed: KEAP1→FASN (too few mutant lines and no signal in Sanger), BAP1→PRKCI (gone in held-out lines, and only one Sanger line had the mutation), and NF2→MAD2L1BP (no signal in held-out or Sanger). All of them came from small groups of 9–14 mutant lines, which probably overstated their effects in the discovery data.

findings.claim: Cancer lines with RB1 damaging mutations depend more on the DYRK1A kinase than other lines, across several lineages; the effect replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=6e-7) and Sanger screens (p=0.007), but it is small in Sanger.
RB1-mutant cancer lines are selectively dependent on the activator E2F3, with a large, robust effect (held-out t=-10.3, Sanger t=-6.9).
KEAP1-mutant lines did not show a reproducible extra dependence on FASN (held-out p=0.04 with only 4 mutant lines; Sanger p=0.69).
BAP1-mutant lines did not show extra dependence on PRKCI in held-out lines (p=0.27), and Sanger could not be tested because only one line had the mutation.
NF2-mutant lines did not show extra dependence on MAD2L1BP (p31comet) in held-out Broad lines (p=0.18) or Sanger screens (p=0.25).
